utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Before we continue, I'd like to make a few observations. First of all, and I'm addressing the Defence, when I commented on the way the cross-examination was conducted last Friday, I am aware that I should have done that in the absence of the witness. This is for the Defence to know that, therefore, I regret that I did it in the presence of the witness. That's point one. Second point is that when we granted three hours last Friday to the Defence, it might have been understood that this is related to problems on sitting Tuesday. It is not. If it would turn out that, for whatever reason, we'd need more time, we'll take that. It's not the -- I would say the Tuesday agenda which is finally determining whether or not more time should be taken. This is not an invitation and not an encouragement to take more time, but I just wanted to make it quite clear that these kind of practical circumstances are not the prevailing considerations and that it's finally the fairness and the facilities for the Defence that are guiding the Chamber in making its determinations. Then my third observation is that we received two motions. The first one on a request for certification of appeal. We considered that motion. Then the other motion we received is a confidential motion on the fourth motion on protective measures. I take it that the Defence has also received that motion. I specifically asked to bring it to the attention of the Defence because if the motion would be granted, then a videolink takes quite some time to prepare. Therefore, if the Defence would be in a position to express itself on this fourth motion, seeking -- well, not mainly protective measures but testimony by videolink and in closed session, I'd like to hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, we appreciate Your Honour's first comment about the comment in the presence of the witness, and we understand that. Secondly, as I'd certainly like to offer my apology if I betrayed my irritation on Friday afternoon. I can't apologise for being irritated, Your Honour. That's another matter, but I can apologise for betraying my irritation, and I realise that the -- what Your Honour said was in fact wrapped in a compliment somewhere, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We gladly accept what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next point is that Your Honour has confirmed it. In fact, for all thoughts we might have about the case, we did not think that the Tuesday timetable was driving that in any case, but thank you anyway, Your Honour. That didn't seem to us to be an issue at all. So far as the motions are concerned, yes, Your Honour has our application on motion in relation to certification. And so far as the other matter is concerned, we are putting in a formal response today, but it might be helpful if I indicate, Your Honour, that we are not objecting to the videolink method of taking evidence in relation to this witness. It seems perfectly sensible in principle, I should say in principle, this Defence team is supportive of videolink evidence, which in many cases is perfectly sensible way of proceeding, we suggest. So you will find us generally supportive of videolink evidence in -- obviously in appropriate cases. There will be some that aren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly we -- I'd just like to say something else which could easily be said in Mr. Mueller's presence but not in the witness's presence. Your Honour, the -- we did and have made it clear at the outset of the cross-examination of Mr. Babic and we continue to, that the Defence -- we do not -- we have not had sufficient time to prepare for cross-examination of Mr. Babic, and that remains the position. It leads to this result, Your Honour: That, as I did on Friday, I am prepared -- I put it this way, Your Honour: I do not object to proceeding with cross-examination of Mr. Babic as best I can, exploring what areas I feel equipped to explore with him, as efficiently as I can manage, given the circumstances. The -- there are two aspects, then, that that leaves. One is complying with my obligation under Rule 90(H) to put such aspects of the Defence case as this witness might be able to help with, comment upon, give evidence upon. Again, I will comply with that obligation as much as I can, but it may be with the benefit of hindsight it will be seen that there are aspects of the case which would be covered by that provision, which ought in different circumstances to have been put, which I won't have been able to put. Secondly, and related to that, is the real possibility, it's always there with any witness in principle, but the real possibility that at some point the Defence will ask for Mr. Babic to be recalled. Now, there's no value in dealing with that in abstract, Your Honour, in any detail this morning, because ex hypothesi what we're talking about is something when we're looking at it in due course we will say this is something that we couldn't reasonably have dealt with at the time but which justifies his being recalled. So that is a bridge which has to be crossed as far as the actual content of any such application were concerned. But specifically in relation to this witness, although it's implicit as an underlying point in relation to any witness, but it normally doesn't arise, but we would like to make that observation to record that there is a distinct possibility in relation to Mr. Babic that that will occur. Because we have been faced with two aspects in a nutshell. One is that Your Honour knows the Defence position in relation to preparation for the case generally, which involves such matters as the context and the wider knowledge of the case, which particularly in relation to Mr. Babic, where it brings in the whole aspect of Croatia, has put the Defence under pressure and difficulty, and specifically in relation to Mr. Babic, the quantity of material, given the enormously high pressure timetable of this case over the last couple of weeks. And Your Honour will be perfectly well aware, I'm sure Your Honours will be aware of the enormous pressures over the last week but wouldn't have lost track of the fact that the week before was an exceptionally heavy week with a number of different aspects that directly related to the trial hearing itself and to wider considerations and looking ahead to the case. So we frankly acknowledge that. We're not just acknowledge it, but assert it, Your Honour, that the alternative, which we have seriously considered, was whether, notwithstanding the exchanges on Friday and where we got to on Friday, whether this morning we could simply say, well, we are not properly ready to proceed with Mr. Babic's cross-examination. But the fact is I believe that -- I'm adopting the criterion that so far as I feel that I can explore particular areas with Mr. Babic safely in the sense that it's my judgement on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik I'm not taking any unwarranted risks by going into those areas of cross-examination. That's one criterion but that leaves the whole area of what areas and what matters I might wish to explore further if we had had more time and opportunity to be ready for his cross-examination. So, Your Honour, on that footing, we do expect to -- I'm not expecting that in 20 minutes time I'm going to say, well, that's as far as I can go. I do want to make it clear to Your Honour that we are proposing to go through quite a lot of ground today. We're proposing to meet Your Honour's time limit and we hope that something valuable and efficient will emerge for this trial out of the next less than three hours. But I think, Your Honour, that's probably as much as I can or need say at the moment in relation to matters which, as I said, ex hypothesi to some extent, can't than be elaborated further for precisely the reasons indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there would be a request for recall of Mr. Babic, in general I would say that the Chamber would be surprised under normal circumstances if there would be a request for a recall of a witness at a later stage where the witness has already been cross-examined. Let me express it in this way, that the Chamber would be less surprised, given the circumstances, if such a request would be ever made, and we'll then seriously consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, but that -- Your Honour, that's a very fair response, if I may say so respectfully, and I think therefore we understand the Trial Chamber and the Defence understand each other in relation to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I got the impression that Mr. Krajisnik wanted to address the Court. Is that a correct impression or is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It seems it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for allowing me to address them very briefly. What I wish to say on this occasion is in fact a request. Whenever you find the possibility, I would appreciate it if you would give me an opportunity to express my concern regarding the preparation of this trial. I am very concerned about the way this trial is moving on. I understand the hearing should begin soon, but I beg you to find the time for my address. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What would be anything in addition to what counsel have already expressed, or would there be something -- or would you like to underline what has been expressed by counsel? That's -- I mean the concerns have been expressed. That's maybe clear to you. But we'll give you an opportunity. Let's leave it to that. I'd rather now start with the examination of the -- the continuation of the cross-examination of Mr. Babic, but we'll find soon a moment where we'll give you an opportunity to further address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am not in a collision, in conflict with my Defence counsel, but I would like to add a few points. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give you an opportunity soon for that. Mr. Mueller may be accompanied into the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. Mueller.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Repositioning you in this courtroom doesn't change your position in any way. Then I'd like to have Mr. Babic escorted into the courtroom, and perhaps we should take care that no one breaks his legs over the lifeline of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm so cautious, Mr. Stewart, because I've seen accidents happen with Ferraris before. Mr. Babic, please be seated. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and I'd also like to remind you to the -- I would say the special attention I paid to these duties when cross-examination started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, my other computer is a Dell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, please proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we are considering a number of different meetings when you were giving evidence on Friday. You have given a number of -- or you have been interviewed on a number of occasions in connection with proceedings against you before this Tribunal, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular, I want to refer you to an interview which you gave on the 11th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is that a slip of the tongue that you said 1992? Because that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is a slip of the tongue, Your Honour. Thank you for -- thank you for pointing that out. 2002, of course, 11th of January, 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's at a time when you were a suspect. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you -- you were being asked, and this is at page 60 of -- for everybody's record, page 60 of the transcript of an interview being conducted on the 11th of January, 2002, and you were being asked about meetings about which you've already given evidence before this Trial Chamber, with Mr. Karadzic. And do you recall, you say there were two meetings that you had in July 1991 on the same day. You first of all met Mr. Milosevic and then Mr. Karadzic and then you went to Celinac and you had a meeting where Mr. Milosevic was not present? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at a meeting with Milosevic and Karadzic in Belgrade on the same day as I met with Karadzic in Celinac, if that's what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And Mr. Milosevic was not present at the second of those meetings, but Mr. Karadzic was; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean in Celinac, then no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The -- and then you -- you've described in evidence -- well, in your statement, you said: "I usually ordered a coffee." This was the meeting with Mr. Milosevic. "But Milosevic insisted we drink whiskey. You know he said: Well, I would -- he said, Let's drink to this, and then he offered us cigars. He had a box of cigars. I don't smoke, so I didn't take a cigar, but Karadzic did take a cigar. He lit it up and put it in his pocket." And you said: "These are the picturesque scenes that I remember." And then you commented that you have more of a visual memory. And then you said: "We resumed our meeting in Celinac." That's near Banja Luka - the same evening, and that meeting, as you've described, was mainly attended by people from the area of Banja Luka. The incident that you've described where Mr. Karadzic, or Dr. Karadzic, it is, rather theatrically used a cigar to represent or indicate to Mr. Izetbegovic and his attitude towards Mr. Izetbegovic, do you say that took place at the meeting in Celinac and not at the earlier meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He put one of Milosevic's cigars into one of his pockets and using that cigar he represented or impersonated Izetbegovic in Celinac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that took place in Celinac and not at the earlier meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I appeared before the Trial Chamber, I described this attempt at drama in Celinac. I also described the conversation in Belgrade. I described the play-acting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just confirm for us this morning, Mr. Babic, what I put to you was that this theatrical performance by Dr. Karadzic took place in Celinac and not at the earlier meeting in Belgrade that same day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Celinac, it was a very theatrical performance on his part, but in Belgrade he behaved decently before Milosevic. He just explained, without gesturing, without play-acting of the kind he did in Celinac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, there's some -- it's a bit ambiguous the answer the witness gave on your question when you said: Mr. Milosevic was not present at the second of those meetings, but Mr. Karadzic was; that's correct, isn't it? Then the answer was: "If you mean in Celinac, then no." It's unclear whether the "no" was about the absence of Mr. Milosevic in Celinac or whether that your statement was not correct. Do I understand your testimony to be that the morning session, or indeed the earlier session was in the presence of Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic, and the second meeting, Mr. Milosevic was absent, Mr. Karadzic was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also -- well, you gave a number of interviews, of course. Another interview in connection with your position as a suspect was on the 15th of January, 2002. So that was just a few days after the one we've been referring to. And the reference to that is at page 12. And the question you were asked by one of the interviewers with the initials AC, that you were asked -- the question is: Why was this meeting in -- and I should say straight away that the transcript says: "Why was this meeting in?????" is the way it's typed out. But we believe it is absolutely clear from the rest of the transcript that it was the Celinac meeting being talked about. It's just that the transcriber apparently wasn't able to identify the name or the word at the time. And we'll proceed on that footing. And you said: "Well, Karadzic, I believe it so that Karadzic proposed these initiatives concerning the two Krajina. This is my impression, but I cannot recall precisely the words. So I was there just standing as a figure at this meeting, because this was a meeting with the people from the Banja Luka region. Here he showed," and then the he is clearly Dr. Karadzic, "he showed his domination and that he is a person who ought to be respected." And then Mr. Mueller, who was present, just commented that you'd already given statements about this meeting. And then it was said. Actually by one of the interviewers -- well, it was actually lead counsel, as it turned out in the case against you, but actually two matters we did not discuss in -- this in relation to his opposing the united Krajina. And one -- and at one point we left open so far is which regions did Karadzic want to unite. And then you said: "I don't know." Counsel doing the interview said: "Did he not specify it in any way." And you said: "So, well, I don't know in what sense, but he indicated that this would be the Serbian areas. This is how I understood it, but precisely what he thought or understood by that, I don't know." And then you were asked: "And did he indicate what would happen in the areas that are mixed, where the Muslims and the Croats were the majority or half-half?" You said: "No, no. I haven't heard." And you were asked then: "Did he mention why he preferred this united Bosnian Serb territories?" And you said: "Well, I have these political -- I make some political assumptions. I do not know whether this was his position." You were asked: "What did he say?" You said: "But, but, he was a political leader." And you -- that's what you said: "But, but, he was a political leader." And then you continued: "I don't know what he said exactly. As I understood it, that he wouldn't like it to this severed from his zones of political interest. This is what I thought." Now, the impression given by your answers in relation to that meeting, Mr. Babic, is that it was not at all clear to you what Dr. Karadzic was saying and what his plans, to use that word, were; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not provide all the information about everything I knew, and at the end of my interviews I did say that I had more to say, more to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then can we move on to the meeting that you have described at the Federation Palace in Belgrade. Your evidence was of a meeting on the 23rd of October. 23rd of October, 1991. You -- on the 30th of November, 2001, you were interviewed, and there are two transcripts on that day. There was earlier in the day, 9.49 a.m., there's a long transcript, 42 pages, and then there's another one. You appear to have resumed after a break to change tapes and get something to eat and so on. And you resumed at 15.03. And then at page 2 of that transcript, you were asked about the meeting in the Federal Palace, the one we've just mentioned. And you were being questioned again. It's Mrs. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff. And she asked you -- this is at the foot of page 3: "And in relation to this meeting in the Presidency, when all the other people were present, including Bosnian Serbs like Karadzic, what was the aim of these people round the table in relation to Yugoslavia and the territories?" And you said: "All these people were supporting this federal Yugoslav option. A delegation of Montenegro was present, but I don't think that Momir Bulatovic was present. I don't know. This can be checked. I think that it was the president of the Montenegrin Assembly and some other people. I think that, if I remember correctly, Bulatovic -- or Momir Bulatovic at a certain point accepted these Hague documents and that Milosevic remained isolated, but then at a certain point, I don't know, was it the assembly or who that -- Bulat [sic] then withdrew his" -- then something inaudible. "And in connection with this meeting, I would like to add something: I don't remember that people were explicitly declaring themselves concerning this. Technically speaking, what was happening was that Branko Kostic was counting -- was calculated." And Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff said: "This 50 that you mentioned already, the 52 per cent", and then you said: "What of 52 per cent for Yugoslavia, of what he knows that" And then you were asked: "Yes, and who from the Bosnian Serbs was there? You mentioned Karadzic. Who else?" And you said: "I can't remember. I can't remember. You see, I was really -- I can't remember. I didn't pay so much attention, because I was preoccupied with this problem of Milosevic and the meeting in Paris. You see, they, they, all these people, as I remember, they were more like a decoration, a backdrop, and a backdrop to that statement, which was then issued to the media." And then Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff went on to ask you about some particular people, whether they were present, including, she said: "What about Martic, Milan Martic? Was he present?" And you said: "I don't think so. I believe not, because I think I would remember it." And then so on, to some other people. So do you agree, Mr. Babic, that, first of all, it's crystal clear from that exchange that your memory of who was or was not at that meeting is a very long way from confident and sure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure. I don't have a visual memory of the whole meeting. I have some feelings and impressions. And as far as my visual memory is concerned, I said exactly who I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also, of course, said who you didn't remember, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's obvious. We don't need to debate or discuss it. It's obvious that among the people you didn't remember was Mr. Krajisnik, because you didn't mention him specifically as having been there. He must have been included in that general category of "you couldn't remember." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visually, I don't remember him, but I do have the impression that he was among the four from Bosnia and Herzegovina, in addition to Vucurevic. It is an impression. I don't have the picture in my mind. I cannot describe it, but that's an impression I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Babic, we are in any case checking to see in the end whether Mr. Krajisnik was wasn't there. I put it to you on Friday that he wasn't, but we are in fact, I should say, we're conducting checks and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we're seeing, because -- I make it clear, we don't regard it a matter of certainty at the moment. But what I put to you is this: That if Mr. Krajisnik was there, then your description of how all these other people were more like a decoration, a backdrop, makes it absolutely clear that he played no significant role at the meeting. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said something to the effect that Branko Kostic was taking the chair, and in that sense I agree with you. I said that the group of people from Bosnia and Herzegovina was representing the Serbs. That was their role. It was the meaning of their presence there, to represent the Serbs, just as I was representing the Serbs of the SAO Krajina. In that sense, our presence there was significant, and technically speaking, the leading role belonged to Branko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You introduce a qualification into your answer, Mr. Babic, so I'm going to press you. In whatever sense, apart from presence at the meeting, if Mr. Krajisnik was at the meeting, but apart from that, in whatever sense, he played no significant part in the meeting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a representative role. I don't remember him playing an active part. As I said before this Trial Chamber when we discussed this matter the first time, I described the way Branko Kostic did his arithmetics. He counted the people who were in favour of a united Yugoslavia, and that's how he reached the figure of 52 per cent. He was counting the republics and the peoples who were in favour of Yugoslavia. What Krajisnik said about Bosnia and Herzegovina, I don't know. The representatives of Montenegro, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the others, represented these peoples who eventually made the sum of 52 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. These -- these -- they're quite unwieldy files on a flimsy -- flimsy lectern, so there's a certain amount of physically moving backwards and forwards of these files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- Mr. Babic, there was no interaction between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik that you can possibly remember from that meeting, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean their contributions at that meeting, what they said?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I mean exactly what I say. There was no interaction between Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik that you can possibly recall from that meeting, whoever was present, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my impression that they were together, they were sitting together. To the right of the chairman, Mr. Kostic, and the other members of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's only, Mr. Babic, you only say that because it's absolutely obvious that if Mr. Krajisnik was at the meeting, he and Dr. Karadzic would have sat near to each other. That's obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my impression the people from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbs, were sitting together in a group. To the left of the chairman, Mr. Kostic. But I don't have the picture in my mind, as I said already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Babic, is this: That it is so obvious and normal that it would have been absolutely extraordinary if whatever Bosnian Serbs were there had not sat somewhere round the table together in a group, wouldn't it? It would have been weird.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you no comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- you gave an interview, as we've indicated, 15th of January, 2002, and at page 26 of the session that began at 17.04, you were asked about the meeting that took place in Belgrade on the 31st of January and the 1st and 2nd of February, 1992. And you said -- well, the introduction to the question -- to the answer was: "Were there occasions in 1992 that you and Karadzic met?" Your answer: "Yes." "Can you tell us how much such occasions there were?" "Well, twice." "Can you describe these?" Your answer: "Yes. The first meeting was a large session of the Presidency of Yugoslavia on the 31st of January, 1st and 2nd February. Then the both of was" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm simply reading what's on the transcript, so when it sounds a business disjointed I'm simply reading what it says. "Then the both of was attended the meeting at the round table in the federal palace. He sat diagonally at the other side of the big table from me with Biljana Plavsic, and I think also that Krajisnik attended it, maybe Koljevic from the leadership. The meeting was chaired by Branko Kostic and Jovic. What is his name, member of the Presidency helped me. Borisav Jovic, the other members," and so on. The -- your reference there to Dr. Karadzic sitting diagonally at the other side of the big table from you with Biljana Plavsic, and then "I think that also Krajisnik attended it," would you agree that that your expression of thinking that Mr. Krajisnik also attended it -- makes it clear that you weren't quite as sure about Makes it clear that you weren't quite as sure about Mr. Krajisnik's attendance as you were about Dr. Karadzic and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I was beginning to remember the situation as the interview was developing, and I must say I didn't know in advance what questions would be asked. And a lot of time had elapsed. And it took me some time to start remembering things, things started coming back. What you quoted was just the beginning of my answer. I was beginning to remember events as I was asked. But I remember the four of them were certainly present, Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, and Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your memory has improved since you were being interviewed on the 15th of January, 2002 in relation to this matter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when I started thinking about these events and these mental pictures, not only did I think about them during the interviews, but in those days and months I went back to the past completely, to the time when these events took place. There were many events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you can now remember anything at all about Mr. Krajisnik's participation, active participation, in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He spoke frequently and repeated the words of the other participants, Dr. Karadzic, Borisav Jovic, Branko Kostic. He toed the same line as they did and he took the floor frequently. I know that for certain because out of the four leaders of the Bosnian Serbs, after the first break, Biljana Plavsic left and the three of them remained. It was a three-day session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just remind ourselves of what you said in the course of the interview, then, on the 15th of January, and this is at page 31 of the transcript. You were asked: "And Mrs. Plavsic, what did she say?" Your answer: "In the first discussion, the first discussion began at 10.00 in the morning on the 31st of January. Everybody had a chance to present their opinions. That was before the first break. Her opinion was different to all others. She was the only one that differed in the sense of wondering how was it if Croatia was not disarming, how come ours were to be disarmed? My opinion was that she was not prepared for the meeting, that she hadn't been briefed, and she honestly -- what she thought after the first break, she was not there any more." Question from Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: "Do you recall anything in relation to Krajisnik? Did he say anything?" Your answer: "No. Specifically, I do not remember. But they all spoke in the same way. Karadzic, Radoman Bozovic was constantly making fun out of us. Everyone agreed except the SAO Krajina." So at that point, Mr. Babic, you had no recollection of Mr. Krajisnik speaking except in the most general sense, that it was apparent to you that there wasn't any disagreement, apart from Mrs. Plavsic's view. Is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is correct, and that's what I said a few minutes ago. So I cannot quote the exact words, but the same position was repeated by Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and the others. That's what I talked about and that's what I said a few minutes ago too. So I cannot quote their exact words, but their positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you now summarise that position that they shared? We're talking about, apart from Mrs. Plavsic, the shared position. How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two matters involved. One was the position itself and the other how this position was imposed on others. The first was to adopt without any modification the security plan for the Krajina, the Vance Plan, as agreed upon by Milosevic, Tudjman, and Kadijevic on the 21st of November, 1991, in Geneva. So that was the core of the matter. Their position was that the plan should be imposed upon the SAO Krajina, or rather, upon me, because I represented the SAO Krajina at the time. So that is what it was all about, to have this position imposed on us through a psychological and physical torture that went on for three days. That is the essence of that position, the essence of that session, and that is the main reason why Momcilo Krajisnik took part in this session too, that this position be imposed on me in particular, even by means of psychological and physical torture. I myself was supposed to adopt the plan regardless of whether others would. So that was the essence of Mr. Krajisnik's position and the things he did, and he agreed on that with everyone except for Mrs. Plavsic. Of course, I exclude here the positions of the government of the SAO Krajina and the representatives of the municipalities of the Krajina who were with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the position was a complex matter, Mr. Babic, but in its essentials, the position was simply this, wasn't it: That you, the leadership of SAO Krajina, you were in a position to disrupt and effectively destroy the implementation of the Vance Plan, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. First of all, we were not and I was not involved in the adoption of that plan. That plan was agreed upon by Milosevic, Tudjman, and Kadijevic, without the Krajina itself. And it did pertain to the Krajina. Secondly, as president of Krajina, I very intensively expounded on the position of the SAO Krajina, seeking for its alteration. When it was adopted, then the Assembly also adopted the plan and Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic, Milan Martic, they actually impeded the implementation of the plan that they had imposed on the Krajina themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, as you've indicated in your answer, the problem number one for you was this: The agreement had been reached without your involvement, so that you felt, didn't you, that in some way it had been done over your head, without properly taking account of your interests and without proper consultation with you. That was your position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your opinion. That's not correct. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you had put it, it is not correct. That plan did not provide sufficient guarantees for the safety and security of the Serb people in the Krajina, and that is what was discussed. It was a security arrangement. During the discussion -- or rather, to put things more precisely, during the public polemic regarding our rejection of that plan, mine in particular, the plan was modified. The Secretary-General of the UN proposed certain modifications with regard to that plan, namely, that Croatian laws and the Croatian legal system would not be applied in the UNPAs, the UN protected areas. And that was the Krajina. That was a success, if I can put it that way, that we achieved during that discussion, but that was the only thing, only that. But this was adopted by the Security Council. We had our own proposals in terms of modification, and that was one of the proposals that was adopted. However, Slobodan Milosevic did not allow any discussion about modification, any discussion about that plan, and that was the point of the meeting in Belgrade. That was its essence, not to allow any discussion of that plan but to have this plan imposed on the Krajina as he and Tudjman had agreed upon it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, with respect, you do not answer my question, not for the first time. I asked you whether, first problem for you was that you felt that in some way this agreement had been reached over your head, without properly taking account of your interests, without proper consultation with you. Now, leaving aside the merits and demerits of the proposal and the plan itself, that is correct, isn't it, Mr. Babic: You did have that feeling, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given an answer to that. It is not correct. This is the second time I'm telling you that this is not correct that that was my first problem. The first problem was that which was of a security and safety nature, and it had to do with the people of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the one doesn't contradict the other. And whether it was your first problem or your second problem. The question, quite simply is: Whether you had the impression that this agreement was reached without sufficient involvement of you and sufficient taking into consideration the interests of the people you represented.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did mention that as a fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it was a fait accompli or not, whether you said it before, this is just the question and I do understand your answer to be yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I wanted to give an answer to the gentleman, the lawyer, that that was not my primary problem. That was the problem that we had found there already when we started discussing the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was, at least, an important problem for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps that's the essence of the whole thing, that the plan that pertained to the people in Krajina was made without the people of the Krajina or without its representatives, by the people who were waging war: Milosevic and Tudjman. So what was only sought was agreement, consent to that. Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the -- is this correct: That the two particular issues about the Vance Plan which were objectionable to you, two essential points, were, first of all, that you felt that it effectively represented a strong move towards an independent Croatia with boundaries drawn that would include your Krajina? That's correct, isn't it? That was a deep concern of yours and the fundamental objection to the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that was not the political arrangement for the Krajina and did not pertain to a political solution. However, in a way, it suggested a political solution without seeking a status for the Krajina prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a political plan. It was a security arrangement. This was on the margins, or rather, it was in addition to that. A political solution was not the main problem then, but a security arrangement. However, what was a problem was that perhaps it could be interpreted in this way: That without a proper agreement, a political solution was being pre-empted. But that was a different matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, some of these other issues could keep Ph.D. students busy for a hundred years. But the position was this, wasn't it: That whether or not it was primarily a security arrangement, the Vance Plan, as far as you were concerned, had that clear political implication of going in the wrong direction, as far as you were concerned, because it was increasing the risk that the boundaries of Croatia would ultimately get drawn to include your Krajina; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, that was not the principle issue. It did not constitute the focus of the problem or the discussion. I was clear. I just sought protection for the Krajina in two ways, with a modified Vance Plan and the presence of the JNA, and the other option was the Vance Plan with the presence of UN troops, with UN protection. If you're really interested in my position at that time. And all of this was for the sake of security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, yes, we are interested. The other major problem related to the other objections was, as you've just mentioned, the fact that the Vance Plan contemplated the withdrawal of the JNA from your Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so was there any other -- I'm sure you had lots of other objections, but was there any other objection to the Vance Plan at -- on the same level, as important as the considerations that we've just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main objection was how the UN would protect the territory, the SAO Krajina, or rather, the people in the SAO Krajina, and how they would make it possible for refugees to return to have a multi-ethnic police, et cetera. Our primary position was: They should be placed on the separation line between the two warring parties, along the lines of the Cyprus model, where the so-called green line existed. That was the proposal. That is how the JNA would remain in that territory, as an armed force, and all the units that were under its command, including the Territorial Defence. However, the plan envisaged total demilitarisation, that is to say the JNA and the Territorial Defence, but it did allow for the possibility of a regional police and the local police. However, our objection was that the plan pertained only to the initial six months and then it was extended to encompass all of a year, and we believe that that was insufficient in view of all of the changes that took place within the international community and the former Yugoslavia. So we evaluated our proposals in the sense that we accepted the demilitarisation of the Krajina in the presence of the protection forces of the UN, but that the UN should impose a kind of protectorate there, that they politically deal with the area before a political solution is found. That was the final position taken by myself and the top people of Krajina. In February, the Security Council passed a decision to implement the plan and we adopted it the way it was worded in the Security Council. We did not level any further objections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, would you agree that this was the position. I'm just about to summarise. What I'm putting to you and ask whether you agree or disagree, that you had a very strong disagreement with -- well, both the Belgrade leadership and the Bosnian Serb leadership about whether the Vance Plan would be, first of all, effective, ultimately, and secondly, whether it was fairly taking account of your interests and your Krajina. Now, so far, you would agree with that so far, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did not agree with the position that they presented, and the position they presented was that the plan should be adopted as it was agreed upon between Milosevic and Tudjman. There weren't any big discussions on their part. They didn't even want to speak about the essence of the security arrangement or about our problems or the problems pertaining to our protection. In a discussion about the plan as such was rejected, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you were asked whether you agreed that you had difficulties with the Belgrade leadership and the Bosnian leadership for the reasons given by Mr. Stewart. Your answer until now is: I would say yes, and then you start explaining why you disagreed with that. You are not asked yet to do that. Mr. Stewart is under time restraint. Would you please listen carefully to his questions and then answer them. And if further information is needed, Mr. Stewart will ask you for it. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. The questions put by the lawyer, by the gentleman, include his own positions. That's why I cannot give mere yes or no answers. I have to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not under all circumstances. It's not necessary that the witness disagrees with the position taken by Defence counsel. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, may I, with respect, endorsing what His Honour says, you can always start with a yes or no and if the Trial Chamber feel that you must in fairness be allowed to elaborate that answer, I'm sure that His Honour will say so. So I invite you to adopt that course. The -- Mr. Babic, would you also agree with this, then: That whatever disagreements there were, and there clearly were, between you and the Belgrade and the Bosnian Serb leadership and possibly others, about the Vance Plan, there was nothing to indicate that the Belgrade leadership and the Bosnian Serb leadership were motivated in their wish to support the Vance Plan by anything other than a wish to achieve a peaceful solution to the Croatian war? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean yes. I think they had other motives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your answer, then, to mean that you don't agree that they were motivated by something other than a wish to achieve a peaceful solution to the Croatian war. That's how I understand your answer. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I wonder if that's coming across correctly or whether I expressed it correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, double negatives always create confusion. I do understand, Mr. Babic, that your answer is that they had an agenda different from reaching a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. It's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- well, let's -- we better take them separately, hadn't we? That's a rhetorical question. The -- Mr. Milosevic, what was his different agenda, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Divide Bosnia with Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Divide Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you say, then, was the different agenda of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. What does this different, additional, mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to see whether I can clarify it for you. The first question was whether everyone tried to achieve peace in the Croatian conflict or whether they had other things in their mind. You now explained what the Belgrade leadership had in mind, apart from reaching a peaceful solution. Now the question is: What did the Bosnian leadership have in mind? What did they have on their agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had a common objective with Slobodan Milosevic. And I must add that their objective was not to attain peace in Croatia. Because two or three months later, they carried out the militarisation of Krajina yet again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your position -- I had specifically asked you about the Bosnian Serbs. Are you saying, then, that the -- they shared Mr. Milosevic's agenda, or object, of dividing Bosnia with Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which bit of Bosnia was Mr. Tudjman to get for Croatia in accordance with the Bosnian Serb leadership agenda?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the area of Bihac, the areas in Herzegovina, the area of Central Bosnia, and I think that at that point in time, all these areas were not very specifically defined by Milosevic and Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you express these views at the three-day meeting in Belgrade at the end of January and beginning of February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what the discussion was about, so my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, correct me. The discussion was about whether you would accept and support the Vance Plan, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan was the question under discussion, but I asked for the possibility to discuss a modification of the plan. But the other side, the Belgrade Bosnian side, asked for this plan to be imposed upon us. That was the topic of this three-day meeting. Only questions related to the security arrangement for Krajina. Yes, and Eastern Slavonia and Western Slavonia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that were a suitable break point for the Trial Chamber, it would certainly fit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart, it is. We'll resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I give an oral decision on the fourth motion for protective measures in the testimony through means of videolink. That's the fourth motion. The motion is granted. Then, Madam Registrar, could you please ... This is just for the information of the parties, because the decision should be given in open session. I'll do that at a later stage. I'll publicly pronounce the decision. So this is just so everyone is aware. Madam Usher, yes, would you please accompany Mr. Mueller into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: While that's happening, does the Trial Chamber -- would you wish to have the formal written response from us in relation to that? We're entirely in Your Honour's hands as to whether we do that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think if you do not oppose the -- I think it's on the record. Perhaps I -- when I pronounced the decision in open session, then I'll first mention the motion, then that there was an oral response by the Defence. We should have gone into open session for that as well. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll pronounce that all in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Every piece of paper saved is also helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Babic. May I instruct you, before we continue, to carefully listen to the questions. You're not here to justify whatever political position was taken at that time, either by you or by anyone else, but just to answer the questions. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to move on to ask you about the meeting which you say took place in Bosanski Novi in either the late summer or autumn of 1992. First question, Mr. Babic, is this: Do you think it's possible that you are mistaken, quite significantly mistaken, about the date when that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I suggest to you that the meeting -- there was, in fact, no such meeting in Bosanski Novi in the late summer or autumn of 1992, but there was such a meeting, and broadly as described by you, broadly, I emphasise, on the 24th of April, 1993, what do you say about that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the meeting in Bosanski Novi, which was held before the session of the joint assembly of Republika Srpska and the Serbian Krajina in Prijedor in end October. It was held, I believe, after the funeral of Jovan Raskovic; that is, it was the first time after March 1992 that I entered the territory of Bosnia. I remember that meeting that was held before the Prijedor assembly session held in October 1992, but it was after my first entry into the territory of Bosnia after the outbreak of the war. That is how I determined the broader time frame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just that when you were interviewed on the 15th -- I'm sorry, on the 16th of January, 2002, and this is at page 7 of the first session, if indeed there was more than one session, you were asked by Mr. Corin, one of the interviewers, investigators, perhaps if I could just ask a couple of follow-up questions on the joint sessions of the Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina sessions in Bosanski Novi and Prijedor. And then you were asked: "Do you recall the date of the session in Bosanski Novi?" And you said: "No, but what I do think is that it was held prior to the one in Prijedor." Now, Mr. Babic, certainly you were saying you thought it was held prior to the one in Prijedor, but you didn't appear certain about that even at that time; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that it was held before the assembly session in Prijedor that was held in end October. I am sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were asked in the continuing -- the very same transcript on the same page, you were asked by Mr. Corin: "Do you recall whether there was a single major topic that was dealt with at that session?" And you said: "I don't remember that there was something particular." You were asked: "Do you recall why the session was held jointly, or the two assemblies?" And you said - I think you were questioning - in Bosanski Novi. Mr. Corin said: "Yes." You said: "I don't remember the reasons. What I do remember was that I was the most isolated figure there. I was sitting in the back of the room alone." Now, does that tie in with your recollection now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked, at page 10 of the same interview, by

utterances.speaker: MRS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "So who had initiated this joint meeting? Do you know that? Was it the Bosnian Serbs or the Croatian Serbs?" And you said: "I don't know who gave the initiative, but formally it was convened by the president of the Assembly." And then you went on: "So it was Paspalj and the other person. Remind me. Krajisnik, Krajisnik." And then: "Was someone present from the federal level or from Serbia?" It doesn't sound from those answers, Mr. Babic, as if you were regarding Mr. Krajisnik as a central figure. You were not even reliably remembering his name at that point, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that you apparently were not even reliably remembering Mr. Krajisnik's name when you were being interviewed at this point?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was a single moment while I was speaking, but it's impossible that I did not remember Krajisnik's name. Maybe I made a pause in answering, but it is absolutely impossible to suggest that I couldn't remember Krajisnik's name. Maybe it was just a brief pause during the interview. Of course I can remember Mr. Krajisnik's name at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on, then. Same transcript, you were asked, very next question: "And was someone present from the federal level or from Serbia?" And you said: "I don't remember." Then you were asked: "Were the military --" and that question seems to have gone perhaps unfinished. And you said: "Well, maybe from Serbia. Then it was Seselj. But then again, I am not sure." And then you were asked about JNA officials. So, now, first of all, at that point you were expressing yourself as not being sure whether Seselj had been there; correct? You acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sure that Seselj was there. I was answering the other questions, I suppose. I suppose that was my answer to the question about representatives from Serbia and the JNA, but I'm certain that Seselj was there. That is in fact my strongest impression from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you -- it was put to you, same interview, page 11, by

utterances.speaker: MRS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "You say you don't recall the topic, but what was it all about?" And then you say: "I can't remember that there was something particular. As I recall this assembly meeting, joint assembly meeting, had no particular topics, specific topics." Does that now accord with your recollection or perhaps non-recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the details. I couldn't remember them then and I don't remember them now, apart from the general discussion. I don't know whether you referred to it, but I was late in arriving for the meeting and I wasn't very familiar with the details or the background material, the preparations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were asked, page 12 of the same transcript, you were asked about Prijedor. You said, page 13: "I shook hands with Karadzic." That's at the Prijedor meeting. "Krajisnik, and I don't know the others who were there." And at page 14 you said you think it was joint -- the session was chaired jointly by Paspalj and Krajisnik. And that's what you remember, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well that it was a joint session, or rather, it was the session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, but there was one common point, the discussion of which was attended also by the representatives of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, only for that one item was it a joint session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said in your interview you think it was joint, the session was chaired jointly by Paspalj and Krajisnik, you're now saying that referred only to one specific part of the meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it was. That joint meeting happened during the session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, and I remember well that we representatives of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, concerning that item of the agenda, the adoption of the declaration on aspirations for unification, were invited to that meeting, and we had a joint meeting during that session, chaired by Momcilo Krajisnik and Paspalj, and I attended that part of the session, that meeting. After the discussion of that item, we left, and there was a break, and after the break, we did not return to the session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so far as the bit of the meeting that was jointly chaired is concerned, would you agree that effectively between the two of them it was in fact Mr. Krajisnik who chaired the meeting, in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the host, in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in relation to that particular meeting, it was absolutely obvious that Mr. Krajisnik was a leader of the meeting, because he chaired it, and would be accorded all the respect and deference due to the chair of that meeting, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, whatever it was called at the time. Mile Paspalj was the president of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and they were co-chairman at this joint meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that in your statement, and I don't think you need have it. It's a tiny bit of it, paragraph 8 of the statement which you confirmed as part of your evidence. You said that "in subsequent years, from 1993 to 1995, I had the opportunity to meet and speak with Krajisnik on a number of occasions." But I think in fact we've only heard about one occasion specifically. How many times do you now say that you met Mr. Krajisnik in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I remember one meeting. In 1994, I don't remember any meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be clear, then. In 1993, the meeting was where and when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Knin, in the summer, the month of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your statement continuing that sentence, the complete sentence is: "In subsequent years, from 1993 and 1995, I had the opportunity to meet and speak with Krajisnik on a number of occasions, and that solidified my understanding." Now, Mr. Babic, we've got what you just said about the visit to Knin, which is unlikely to be in dispute, and you also re-comment your evidence of having sat next to Mr. Krajisnik at dinner in Pale in 1995. But would you agree that doesn't seem to be very much to provide solidification of any understanding of Mr. Krajisnik's role, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was enough for me to understand what I was seeing and what I heard from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, clear -- Mr. Babic, what I suggest to you is that your statement and your evidence are exaggerating what you know about Mr. Krajisnik and what you have ever seen and observed about Mr. Krajisnik. On reflection, do you think that perhaps that's a fair suggestion to put to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that it's an exaggeration. That's what I know about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say in your statement Karadzic and Krajisnik seemed to interact as equals, Mr. Babic, would you agree that your description of all these various meetings and events makes it crystal clear that they were not equals, that Mr. Karadzic was a boss? Wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they were always together. If I go over all of my meetings with Mr. Krajisnik, he was always with Mr. Karadzic. They were always a team, the two of them. They always agreed and propounded the same opinion. What I heard from other people indicates that in certain matters, Krajisnik was even stronger than Karadzic in Republika Srpska. Even that I heard from others. Karadzic may have had more charisma, was more theatrical in demeanour, but I view them as two equal, very close people. It is a twosome where both members were very close. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we take it, Mr. Babic, that as far as your own observation of the interaction between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic is concerned, that what you have been able to tell the Trial Chamber so far about what you saw and heard and where you were is the full extent of your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say everything that I knew. I met with Mr. Krajisnik in 1995 several times during long sessions, where we talked a lot. I heard a lot about him from others, including Aleksa Buha, the foreign minister of Republika Srpska, in November 1994. I heard many important things about Mr. Krajisnik. That is to say, I did not say everything that I know about Mr. Krajisnik. I haven't said it so far before this Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we have -- just to make it clear, have we covered, as far as you're concerned, all your firsthand observation and knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't covered everything that I know about him. I learned a lot about him in May 1995, things that we haven't discussed here. Firsthand, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Babic, I want to make it absolutely clear. I'm not asking you now about anything you have heard from anybody else, all right, so that you and I might both know things about the president of the United States without ever having, in my case certainly, ever having met him. But -- so I'm not talking about that sort of thing. I'm talking about your own firsthand knowledge and dealings with Mr. Krajisnik. Do you say there is anything else of significance in that category that you have not told the Trial Chamber about in the two or three days that you've been giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only add to the evidence I have given so far. My knowledge was strengthened in 1995, during the meeting in Pale, for instance, the meeting in May, the 17th of May, in Bijeljina, the 21st in Banja Luka, the 31st in Bijeljina again. On those occasions, I had meetings with Krajisnik in person. I learned more about his position and about his union with Karadzic. I learnt that they were both equal forces with different kinds of temperament, but I was able to determine that they were very close and equal in strength. I viewed them as a pair, as a twosome. And they expressed their views, in fact, their same view, in different ways. One was a charismatic person, extrovert and theatrical, whereas Krajisnik was decisive, more business-like, and calm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the discussion that you've told the Trial Chamber about that you had with Mr. Krajisnik when you sat next to each other at dinner in Pale in 1995, was that the only occasion on which you had anything like a private, two-person discussion with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with Mr. Krajisnik in tete-a-tetes and in very closed meetings in 1995, in Bijeljina, in the 21st of May in Banja Luka, and the 31st of May again in Bijeljina. I believe that at those meetings, including the one in January in Pale, I completed my picture about Mr. Krajisnik and the relationships within the leadership of Republika Srpska, and I gained a very clear picture about all of this. So the answer to your question is yes, I did have more opportunity after January 1995 to be with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Babic, let's get it clear. You use the phrase tete-a-tete, which --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's what you said. I used the expression --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. This is a literal interpretation. Four eyes, plus another pair of eyes, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, all right. I didn't get all the eyes there, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- apart from Pale, have you -- that dinner, have you ever in your life had a conversation with Mr. Krajisnik - apart from good morning, that sort of thing, not really a conversation - have you ever had a conversation with Mr. Krajisnik to which the only parties and the only people who could hear what was being said were you and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not any meetings where we were alone together. Even the meeting in Pale was not one when we were alone, the two of us. I was never alone with him. There were always other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the one in Pale, though, the dinner was different, wasn't it, in this sense, do you agree: That at least sitting next to each other at dinner, even with other people at the table, you were able in the normal way to have a conversation which was private to the two of you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I cannot judge how much other people were able to hear. Our discussion was not secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the way -- you've given some evidence about this, and then you also discuss this in your interview on the 19th of February, 2002. This is at page 8 of the first transcript there. And you were being asked by Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff -- well, it doesn't really matter. I can start with your answer towards the foot of this page. "So I understood the basis of all this that Stanisic and Milosevic wanted to have this division of the Krajinas, one of the Knin area and the Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia, and why was this conviction of mine even reinforced? In January 1995, I heard from Momcilo Krajisnik another -- he uttered something rather foolish, that they would get on the basis of us 6 per cent more territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina means 6 per cent more than the 49 per cent, so my conclusion is that there is something terribly wrong." And just to put it in context, we know, don't we, and we've heard this was the percentage being proposed by the -- in the context of the international negotiations, by the contact group? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were further interviewed, in fact you were interviewed over several days. Then you were being further interviewed on the 22nd of February, 2002. Excuse me one moment. You said, page 4: "As far as this harbour, this court is concerned, this came up in connection with the plan of the contact group. It was on that occasion I heard Biljana Plavsic saying how the Bosnian Krajina would come, the Republika Srpska, the Republika Srpska would come to the cost in the area of the cliffs of Konavle." That's obviously a misprint, the coast. "That she said Konavle, the cliffs of Konavle south of Dubrovnik towards, south of Dubrovnik Montenegro. When did she say that? When did you hear that?" That's the question. Your answer: "It was in 1995 when the contact group plan was discussed, but it wasn't the plan of the contact group. This was their idea they developed in Pale." But where did she say that and were you present? She made a public statement in the holidays somewhere. And then you were asked by -- just skipping a couple of lines, you were asked by Ms. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff: "And the objective, do you know what the objective was in relation to Sarajevo? Did you hear that?" Your answer: "Well, I don't know, but they were always speaking about Serbian Sarajevo. Well, they spoke of Sarajevo, of a part of Sarajevo which would be Serbian, or a part where they would build a new Sarajevo or something like that. This is what I heard in winter 1995 from them, how they intend to build a new Sarajevo." Question: "When you say they, who are they? With whom did you speak?" Your answer: "I think it was mostly Krajisnik who spoke about it." Question: "Publicly or to you?" Your answer: "We were -- well, we had a social evening. We had a dinner. So I heard two things from him, and it was a bit of a conviction. I didn't understand what he was referring to, and he said: We don't need Sarajevo. Belgrade is enough for us. So I didn't quite understand. He was speaking on the one hand of this new Sarajevo. They don't need Sarajevo, and that Belgrade is -- suffices for them." Question: "Who was saying this?" Answer: "Krajisnik, Momcilo Krajisnik." Question: "And where did this talk take place?" Answer: "It was in Pale, in a hotel, at the beginning of 1995." So, Mr. Babic, what you were saying there, and I ask whether you feel able to confirm this now, was that you -- it wasn't at all clear to you what Mr. Krajisnik was suggesting when you had that dinner conversation, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was crystal clear to me. I had prior information about Mr. Krajisnik that I received from Buha on the 20th November 1994, which is a month or a month and a half prior to that meeting. So I had some knowledge about the conduct and the opinion of Mr. Krajisnik on the division of territory and the transfer of population. But that game of his, this dribbling and this habit to wrap his ideas into different words, the pretence, was not clear to me. I'm sorry, of course, from Sarajevo. He said that Serbs had Belgrade and they don't need Sarajevo, but I know that later they accused Milosevic, Bosnian Serbs accused Milosevic of having sold Sarajevo. So there was this kind of hypocrisy, two-timing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it was so clear to you what Mr. Krajisnik had been saying at that dinner, why did you say in the course of the interview that it wasn't clear?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not say everything in the interview. I've already said that. To the investigators, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They also jumped from one topic to the other. Perhaps I did not always manage to link things up for them, and thus to present an entity. With the permission of the Court, perhaps I could clarify matters and perhaps I could say a bit more about that meeting and about what Krajisnik had said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could -- I'm not -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What permission the Court gives is in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially since the witness offers to tell us more about what Mr. Krajisnik said. That's different from opinion and conclusions. Please tell us what Mr. Krajisnik said, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I would just like to say first of all what I knew about what Mr. Krajisnik said. Before November 1994, Mr. Aleksa Buha, the then foreign minister of Republika Srpska, said about the meeting between the Krajisnik and Karadzic with the representatives of the Croatian government that had to do with the division of Bosnia and the relocation of the population. What happened after that was my meeting at Pale. So I knew exactly what Krajisnik was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you asked whether you could say a bit more about that meeting and about what Krajisnik had said. I gave permission to you to tell us about specifically what Mr. Krajisnik said. So would you please limit yourself to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat what I said, Your Honour, at the previous sessions before this Court, at the previous sittings, and what is not being quoted now. Mr. Krajisnik -- I mean, first of all, we talked extensively about different subjects, about different things that were going on in Bosnia, about their positions during the negotiations, et cetera. Then I can repeat what I already said. He made a speech about Sarajevo, that in Sarajevo, the ethnic communities always lived separately. Everyone in their own part of town, that they had kept Serb Sarajevo and that he was prepared to give up on this Serb Sarajevo of his, that they had guarded, because the Serbs need only one capital. They don't need two. And their one capital is Belgrade. And that was actually the introduction leading to the main thing that he wanted to tell me. That is the way I understood this. Basically, that he as a person from Sarajevo was not sorry to give up on his Serb Sarajevo and that I should not be sorry to give up on the Serb Krajina, because he said in the context of the negotiations that they had with the contact group that the Americans would give them 6 per cent to the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina, actually, 6 per cent, an additional 6 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in exchange for Sarajevo. Those were the details of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's in your evidence already. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
