utterances.text: The contradiction that you referred to in the interview, then, was the contradiction, was it, between the idea of giving up Sarajevo altogether, but at the same time, intending to build a new Sarajevo? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only in that sense, but also in terms of what I learned later, namely, they were accusing Milosevic that he had sold Sarajevo. But I heard from Krajisnik before the Dayton Agreement, that is to say, almost a year before the Dayton Agreement, that they were prepared to give up on Sarajevo. Those are the two contradictions that I heard. This is primarily what I had in mind, this accusing of Milosevic, that he had sold Sarajevo, their Sarajevo, in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- I'll put Mr. Krajisnik's position to you, Mr. Babic, which is this: That there were about 180.000 Serbs in Sarajevo at the time. Does that accord with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give the exact figure. A large number of Serbs also in percentage terms, lived in Sarajevo. I know that not a single ethnicity was a majority in Sarajevo, but a large percentage of Serbs did live in Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And that it is inconceivable that at that time, in 1995, that Mr. Krajisnik would have seriously considered giving up effectively that population of Sarajevo as residents of Sarajevo in return for a percentage, being 6 per cent, of Bosnia and Herzegovina overall. That's what Mr. Krajisnik says. Do we simply take it that you flatly disagree with that, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically assert what I've already said. What Krajisnik's position was in January 1995. It is the opposite of what you said just now, and it's not at the expense of Sarajevo that he wanted to get an additional 6 per cent of Sarajevo, but rather at the expense of the territory of the SAO Krajina, which was part of the Serb Krajina at the time, and Western Slavonia. That is what was discussed. That is the kind of exchange he wanted, 6 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina for SAO Krajina and Western Slavonia. Sarajevo was an addition, by the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, let's be clear that your evidence is that it was both. We understand that. Your evidence is that Mr. Krajisnik was suggesting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. both the giving up of your Krajina and Sarajevo. You've made that perfectly clear. Mr. Babic, there's no earthly reason, is there, why Mr. Krajisnik, even if that had been, which he says it wasn't, his thinking at that time, there's no earthly reason why he would have shared that with you, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a reason for that, just as you had put it. 180.000 Serbs. I don't know how many actually lived in Sarajevo. And that is his birthplace, Sarajevo. So it's his own town and he was attached to it. That was a major sacrifice for him. That's what he said to me. And he was prepared to give up on that. He was prepared to make the sacrifice, but then I was also supposed to make a sacrifice to give up on my SAO Krajina. That's the context in which he said this. He was quite clear in terms of what he wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'd like to ask one question in between to better understand the testimony of the witness. Mr. Babic, when you say "give up Sarajevo," how did you understand this at that time, to give up the part under the control of the Serbs at that time, which was a part of Sarajevo, or to give up all aspirations on making Sarajevo the -- well, the capital of Republika Srpska? How did you understand? What did that mean to you, to give up Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first thing you said, Your Honour, that is to say that they should give up on that part of Sarajevo that they held at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that you made such a suggestion to Mr. Krajisnik rather than his raising it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, heaven forbid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something else altogether, Mr. Babic. In late 1991, and I'm talking about the very end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, would you have seen yourself, and do you see yourself now, as at that time, as a peacemaker?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said what I was at the time. At that time I was a Serb ethno-egoist. I was not in favour of the war, and from that point of view I was a peacemaker. But I was also concerned about the Serbs, the fate of the Serbs from the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it right to say that your concerns, as you just described them, went hand in hand with a continuing willingness to take necessary military action in your Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the end of 1991 and 1992, military activity had ceased in the Krajina at that time, for the most part. As for previous military activities, I spoke about that at considerable length in the Milosevic trial and before this Trial Chamber, and it was also referred to in my own trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular, do you recall giving a military order on the 26th of December, 1991 to move your forces up in readiness for action against Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. That was shown to me. And as far as I can remember, I think that I gave an explanation for that, that this document had been simply pushed over to me so that I would place my signature on it and thus be compromised from a political point of view. There was no movement of cannons or other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to show you this document, Your Honour. We've got copies of it. I don't need to hand the witness the English version of it. I have the original or copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that document would get number --?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D16.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I have an English transaction, Mr. Babic, but it's a very short document. It might be because it's incomplete and has question marks and bits missing, so perhaps I might just invite you to read it and then we shall get the English translation from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate that, Your Honour. It's a very short document. I hope that isn't a major problem. I'm told they do have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is a very short document, as a matter of fact. If you'd just read it slowly, Mr. Babic. And I take it, Mr. Stewart, that we could limit ourselves to the content -- or would you have all the headings be read as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't need the headings read, Your Honour, if the Trial Chamber's not concerned about that. But the document is in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please start reading where it says "one" and then ... Perhaps you read -- start reading where it says "Commander of" and then the 3rd operative zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "To the command of the 3rd Operations Zone. Number 1, carry out transfer of VP battery, 130 millimetres, to the broader area of S. Madjeri, S. Gradac. Lijevo Sredicko, in readiness for action against the target (Zagreb). X equals 74800 [as interpreted], Y equals 76000, Z equal 180. Readiness for action the 27th of December at 12.00. Expenditure of ammunition 0.5 b/k. Report on readiness at 1100 hours. Signature of the commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, Dr. Milan Babic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic, there's no doubt, is there, this is a document that you signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution, yes. I was president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was signed either on the 26th of December actually or so close that it makes no difference; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 26th of December, 1991. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm simply seeking to confirm is there's no reason to doubt the accuracy of the date is there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was president of the Republic, on the 19th of December I became president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understood what you were signing; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is not whether you remember that, but the main question is whether you understood what you signed. That means if you read such kind of a document, whether you do understand what it says. Of course, whether you now specifically remember on what you understood when you signed it is perhaps a further detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's -- with respect to His Honour, I endorse what he just said, Mr. Babic, let's take it in stages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have any difficulty understanding what this document says, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wouldn't have had any difficulty understanding it in December 1991 if you'd read it, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said: I do not recall the content or the moment of reading it, but most probably the answer would be yes. But I do not remember this, so perhaps I can say yes. But I do not recall this particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection or can you say who would have invited you to sign this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in a package of documents. Somebody from the Main Staff, Colonel Maksic, I think, brought this in for my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we be clear what you're saying, Mr. Babic. Is there a suggestion implicit in what you're saying that this order was in some way slipped past you without you appreciating what it was you were authorising?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something, and you can put that on one side, Mr. Babic - something you said in relation to Kijevo. On Thursday last week, which is Thursday, the 3rd of June, at page 35 of the uncorrected transcript, you've talked about - this is at line 6 - an ultimatum given to the villagers of Kijevo to leave before - these are your words - the artillery barrage actually forced them to leave. Is that right? That was the question. And you said: "Yes. Initially the ultimatum was issued by Martic, several days before the attack of the JNA artillery. I personally protested against this, but I was president of the municipality and the prime minister of the government. However, regardless of my protests, some ten days later, the JNA attack ensued. Following that, I received the information that milicija, Martic's men, and the local TO also participated in the attack." Now, first of all, let us look at that ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm handing in is -- there are two documents. There's a copy of the B/C/S version, which is on a single sheet, and then there is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to just refresh your memory, Mr. Babic, by reading the B/C/S version to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would the original get number D17 and the translation, which is a draft translation, D17.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you've had a chance to read that, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about this on the 13th of January, 2002 in your interview, at page 15 of the first transcript of that day. And in fact, it starts at page 14. I'll start at line 20: "As far as Kijevo is concerned, later I heard that both the army and the Krajina police had information that in Kijevo a police station would be set up by the Ministry of Interior of Croatia." This was in April. This would have been April 1991. I just add the year as a comment myself. "So JNA was already deployed around Kijevo and I assume that Martic also knew this because he was in contact with the military intelligence. I don't believe that they did not inform him about it, and I don't think that -- I don't think that they stopped in any way the police administration from Sibenik to set up its police station in Kijevo, and this police station existed a few months and, and a few months later, Martic issues an ultimatum that they have to withdraw from Kijevo, and this was a publicly issued ultimatum. I don't know -- I don't remember exactly what was published exactly in this ultimatum, but I thought it was an ultimatum to everyone in Kijevo. As I saw it, he made a threat to the entire population of Kijevo. So it wasn't -- I didn't see it only as a correspondence between the police. As I interpreted it, it had a more forcible meeting, and then at risking an internal conflict in Krajina, that would conflict this Krajina. I then made a public statement in the sense more or less that the armed forces in Krajina, irrespective of this, Martic's ultimatum to the police station in Kijevo, the armed forces of Krajina would not disturb, violate the cease-fire. There was already an agreement in a sense between, I believe, the federal bodies and the Croatian bodies, so there was an agreement which prevailed at the time. So this was the form in which I expressed my opposition." And then, after a couple of exchanges, which are not central: "So I was risking attacks at my personality. I was risking it both from the public and the people who had the weapons in Krajina. They could go against me, but nonetheless I made this public statement, so I thought it would be less of a risk that somebody would attack me than to have a fire erupt here." And Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff asked you: "Why did you simply not order Martic? Because you were the president. Why didn't you order?" And you said: "Well, it didn't work like that. It didn't function like that. That's the problem. I couldn't issue orders to him. I was the president of the government, the prime minister, and he, as a minister, was accountable to the prime minister. But this was only -- it was legally, formally -- I didn't have the means to order. I didn't have the power. He had it. I only had the words. He had the armed force, the armed police, the special police. He had a monopoly of power." And you were asked: "Okay. I understand that. Did you ever try?" Your answer: Well, I tried with some political manoeuvres to limit him." Question: "Did you ever try directly?" Martic: "You can't do that." You: "Well I didn't do it but that was the moment I could have said it personally." Interviewer says: "Then." And you say: "But I was I was aware it wasn't him. He wasn't the one" -- Interviewer: "But if you never tried how do you know he wouldn't have obeyed you." Your answer: "Well this was public communication. This was stronger. Here I asked the public for its help, expecting that the public, which I invited to help, that they would influence him, which was the type of -- this was the way communication went. We never talked about these things. He was also physically in another premise."

utterances.speaker: MRS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "Did you -- you if you didn't have the power, did you try to get help to stop Martic from Milosevic, who you said was the boss, to stop the conflict in Kijevo?" You: "No. I didn't talk to anybody."

utterances.speaker: MRS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "But why?" You said: "I assumed they wouldn't take the risk, they wouldn't risk it. I assumed that they wouldn't risk going into a conflict if in Krajina there is the political position that we will not go into a conflict."

utterances.speaker: MRS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "And they is who?" You answered: "Martic, the police." Mr. Babic, you twice in the last 10, 15 minutes, you do seem, do you agree now on reflection, to have a marked reluctance to accept responsibility for your actions? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that statement before the investigators in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's be very specific. You include, for example, here in your statement that Martic was also physically in another premise. Was that being suggested by you as some reason why you couldn't and didn't try to stop him and try to issue any order to him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that. I mentioned the reasons already. He had true power. I had only declarative power. And also I had the public. But he had true power, and also the structure that protected him, Stanisic and Milosevic. That's what it's all about. And they practically kept him under their control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to show you another document, which is -- you can put that one on the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're handing up two documents, or two clips of documents. One is a letter, an open letter written by Mr. Milosevic, and it's addressed to Mr. Babic, although it's an open letter. And then -- that's dated the 8th of January, 1992. And then the other document is -- it's headed "reply to the open letter from the president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic," which is a reply from Mr. Babic. I'd just like to clarify one thing, Your Honour. Your Honour, I was just confirming that the translations are as received by us from the Prosecution. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that the first letter of the 8th of January you provide them in two versions, the one is the original one and the other one is a publication about -- or -- because I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It got fully reported in the newspaper. The text seems to have been fully reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the same text?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it's, for practical purposes, it seems to come to the same thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the translation on the very top -- well, Mr. Babic, of course, can work from the original B/C/S versions of both these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just first ask Madam Registrar to provide numbers to me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the letter of the 8th of January, written by Slobodan Milosevic. And then ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the reply to the open letter, D19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And I point out that both cases we have the -- what seems to be the original and what seems to be the publication of that same letter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- well, I -- I can't take it too quickly, because I have to remember to go at a suitable pace for the interpreters, Mr. Babic. But the letter from -- open letter to you from Mr. Milosevic, he says: "I feel it my obligation and responsibility to express my disagreement with your position that you do not want the UN peacekeeping force to protect the territory of Krajina under the Cyrus Vance plan. Rejecting protection by the UN peacekeeping force endangers the most important interests of the Serbian people because it really means refusing to put an immediate end to the loss of human life and abandoning the path of peace in solving the crisis. The sole purpose of the UN presence is to maintain peace. I know that you were informed in detail at the Yugoslav Presidency about the Cyrus Vance plan, which specifies that the presence of the UN peacekeeping forces does not prejudice political solutions and that their task is to prevent any military formations or armed groups from entering UN-protected territories. You were also informed that the only armed formation in those territories, in addition to the peacekeeping forces, would be the local police, which completely guarantees peace and safety for all citizens. I thus consider your negative attitude utterly irresponsible. You should show that the people are making sacrifices to protect themselves from genocide and that they were making sacrifices to protect their freedom and safety, but they should not make sacrifices because of the vanity of any politician. If battles were fought for a just and honourable purpose, the freedom and safety of the people in the Krajinas and their protection from the genocide they were exposed to, then one cannot be against a resolute step towards that goal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask you: Are you going to read the whole text?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem I have is this. I don't particularly want to, in a sense. On the other hand, it's -- I wish to be fair to the witness in enabling -- I'm in Your Honour's hands. I just wish to be fair to him before we get to his reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the assumption that the cross-examination will not be concluded until the next break, I would like to invite the witness to read or perhaps to reread, because he might have read it before, to reread this correspondence and perhaps you could try to indicate in one or two lines what the correspondence is about and then ask questions to him after the break on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I may not be very much longer, but that would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you'd read the two letters as a whole, then it would take us considerable time, I take it, especially as the so highly appreciated slow pace you are doing it. So, therefore, the break, especially the second break, could be taken earlier or later. It could even be taken now. The witness could then be invited to read it, to reread it, you spend one or two lines on the correspondence as such, for example, that Mr. Milosevic is criticising Mr. Babic on the position he takes in respect of the Cyrus Vance plan, and then you could ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, Your Honour, it would -- I don't have very much further to go. It probably would be convenient, then, if we were to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour indicated that as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could do that. We could have the break now until 25 minutes to 1.00, and we would then have -- I'm not saying for your cross-examination, but at least we would have in Court another 70 minutes. We'll then adjourn for 20 minutes. We'll resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, Mr. Mueller may be accompanied into the courtroom, and Mr. Babic may be escorted into the courtroom at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Babic. You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you've had a -- you've taken the opportunity of reading both these letters during the break, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just confirm: Mr. Milosevic's letter to you was an open letter. Was your reply to him also written as an open letter, available for publication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic's letter was promulgated on the television on the 8th first, and then it was published in the newspapers on the 9th, and only after that was it sent to me, or rather, was received by me in an envelope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't entirely my question, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to carefully listen to the question. The question was whether you, when you wrote the letter, you intended it to be published as well. That was the question. Your answer was about when you received the letter by Mr. Milosevic, that is, after publication. So the question is: When you wrote your letter, did you intend it to be published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, just taking this particular aspect fairly quickly to avoid repetition, we see the fourth paragraph of your letter. You identify your objection to the constitutional and legal system of Croatia being applied in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Then later in that paragraph, a few lines down, you express your objection to the six-month period. And you also, over the page, in the middle of the second page, short paragraph right in the middle: "Considering the given facts after the withdrawal of the United Nations forces, any action by the Yugoslav army, should it exist in such a situation, would be regarded as aggression." And of course that's in circumstances where the JNA would have already withdrawn. So can we agree that those particular bits, they really encapsulate -- it's more widely expressed in the letter, but they encapsulate the essential points of your disagreement over the plan itself, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, at the foot of the first page, you put your alternative proposal, that's your proposal, the other version, including the use of Blue Helmets, or the Blue Helmets, is of course what I mean, along the line of fire between -- and then you say: "The Croatian neo-Nazi aggressors and the defensive armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." Did you regard it as helpful in a letter specifically written with a view to publication to make reference to Croatian neo-Nazi aggressors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, that was the terminology in use, and it reflected the prevailing situation. The frame of mind and the state of our consciousness. And it also reflected the vocabulary of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And similarly, then, in the last paragraph of your letter, where you refer to "the roots of evil that the Croatian Ustasha are inflicting on us." Same applies to that, does it? It was prevailing language and it reflected your views and feelings at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the reality that it was inflammatory language designed for the -- to keep your own people in your own Krajina happy?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not used for that purpose. It was reflective of my feelings and my views. But it did have the effect that you mention. In that sense, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the first complete paragraph on the second page, you say: "As regards of the term of the peacekeeping mission which has been determined to be only six months, we are not ready to be disarmed, to leave our destiny in the uncertain hands of others." Is it fair to summarise that as meaning: We shall fight on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We do not agree. We will continue to fight, maybe. Maybe. Just tell me where that particular passage is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You don't agree. That's all right. The bottom of the first page of your letter, then, the proposal we -- your alternative Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. proposal we looked at a moment ago, then, about the deployment of the Blue Helmets along the line of fire, and so on, that was at the time, was it not, Mr. Babic, an absolutely unreal alternative which had no practical prospect of being accepted by the necessary parties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with you. It was the first proposal and it was in fact mentioned by Borisav Jovic in his request to the United Nations for their engagement. It was the first option that was in circulation even before Milosevic and Kadijevic signed this second version and the possibility that the plan would be modified was open. Mr. Goulding was present in Belgrade on the 27th of January and I talked to him. It was a couple of days before this session. Mr. -- I'm sorry. We were talking about the letter, and I have already moved on to the session. I was talking about Mr. Goulding, the under-secretary for peace operations. The answer to your question is that there was a possibility to contemplate, and even to achieve, this deployment of peacekeeping forces, because approval was sought from Krajina for the plan. Krajina was asked, and that's how I understood it, that it was an open possibility for us to make proposals. And then what I just mentioned happened. The under-secretary for peace operations, Marek Goulding arrived and it was discussed, and that was followed by a session of the presidents

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The position was this, Mr. Babic, wasn't it: There was not a chance in the real world that Mr. Tudjman would sign up to your alternative proposal here, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that moment, it was clear that Milosevic does not want to change his agreement with Tudjman either. That's what I understood. Tudjman also stated, on more than one occasion, that the Croatian authorities would immediately take control of the Serbian municipalities in Krajina, and so on and so forth, and one of our reactions is stated in the letter, namely, that we do not accept the validity of Croatian laws on our territory, and this was followed by the report of the general secretary of the United Nations to the Security Council and the Security Council adopted the decision that Croatian laws would not apply on the territory of the Krajina. This is the context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You choose once again not to answer my question, Mr. Babic, but I'm just going to leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Would you please repeat. I did not wish to not answer your question. Even though you seem to think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, let's not debate it. I'll put it to you. Please listen carefully and then answer. I put it to you: There was not a chance in the real world that Mr. Tudjman would sign up to your alternative proposal.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that proposal for modification was imposed on him by the Security Council and he accepted it. It is true that he accepted it. So the possibility for Tudjman to change his stand existed, and he did change it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is correction and amendment of this plan. One of the amendments to this plan, namely, the modification of the plan that pertains to the application of Croatian laws in the Serbian municipalities in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The use of the Blue Helmets along the line of fire, as you describe it, no chance of acceptance of that by Mr. Tudjman; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought there was a chance. It would be accepted. That's why I spoke about it. It was a model currently in application in Cyprus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you, then, the letter which you looked at before. It's a letter of the 19th of December, 1991 that Mr. Krajisnik wrote, and that was -- it was part of an exhibit to Mr. Treanor's -- or brought up in the course of Mr. Treanor's evidence, Your Honour. The Exhibit number is P65 and it had been bundle 6, or folder 6, page 67 from Mr. Treanor's documents. The witness was shown it in the course of his examination-in-chief. So it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you still have copies, Mr. Stewart? Because we do not always bring the 18 binders of Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, no. I understand that, Your Honour. It's a particular document that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No. I do understand. But could it otherwise be put on the ELMO? Do we have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can do that, Your Honour. Tab 67, I think it is. Your Honour, I'd simply like to say, it's one of those -- while it is happening, one of those practical things that Ms. Cmeric has done a heroic job with photocopying. May I just say the face of the fact that she and I arrived about 20 to 8.00 this morning to find the photocopier was once again out of the action in the Defence room. This is a constant problem for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It will be put, then, on the ELMO. Is there one copy to be put on the ELMO? And it is a letter, Mr. Babic, of the 19th of December, 1991, in which Mr. Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, responds to an invitation to be present on the, as it is said, the historic occasion of the proclamation of the Serbian autonomous region of the Krajina, and unfortunately he's unable to attend. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic, first of all, this is one of those effusive letters which is customarily written by political -- by politicians to other politicians on the occasion of successful elections, establishment of new institutions, significant appointments, that -- it's basically that sort of letter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you also agree that, maybe not uniquely as a people and as a nation, but it's a very Serbian approach to write in these quite flowery, enthusiastic terms, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is flowery. It is a political stance that was held at the time by Mr. Krajisnik, and not only Mr. Krajisnik; many others too. It is not particularly flowery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or effusive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, perhaps it highlights the point, and I'm treading a delicate line. This is not in any way -- there are different cultures. This is not intended in the least bit offensively. Please understand that. The very fact that you don't see it as flowery supports the fact, doesn't it, that this is a normal sort of language and normal sort of tone for a letter written on such an occasion between Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no multitude of such occasions. This was a singular occasion of the creation of Serbian Krajina. This is a political letter dedicated to a specific political moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just that you -- the way you dealt with this in your statement and the way you dealt with it in your evidence, Mr. Babic, you were plainly adopting a negative view of this letter, regarding it, as the way you described it, as an inappropriate letter for Mr. Krajisnik to have written. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand where you find this interpretation. I think this was absolutely appropriate and completely consistent with the stances propounded by Mr. Krajisnik at the time. I don't see what you find inappropriate about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are we -- Mr. Babic, are you saying that you don't regard this letter as inappropriate in its content and its tone for the occasion on which it was written?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is completely consonant with the occasion on which it was sent and with the general political views that prevailed at the time and the general situation. It clearly expresses a certain political stand concerning the prevailing circumstances, if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I just want to ask you about intercepts. You were asked particularly about one intercept relating to a conversation that apparently took place in June 1991. The reference is last Wednesday, the 2nd of June, page 82 of the transcript - between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Curtis. And you had listened to it and you had been able, it seems, to identify the participants. And you gave evidence that the references to flour and salt and supermarkets and so on, that it was a superficially coded conversation, it had to do with delivery of weapons. May I ask you -- well, I'm sure I may. Mr. Babic, what do you know that enables you to tell the Trial Chamber any more about this intercept and its meaning than can be got by anybody reading it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the background, the circumstances, the participants, the events, the terminology, the people, the time when this took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as -- as a whole other lot of intercepts that we didn't go to specifically, but they're scheduled as part of your evidence, so far as those other intercepts are concerned, now you say, of course, that you know the people involved. Do you agree that in most cases, what you were telling the Tribunal in that schedule can largely be gleaned simply from reading the text of the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that these texts confirm what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you say that in relation to any of those intercepts that you have -- those other intercepts, you have some specific, special piece of knowledge in relation to the content of that intercept that enables you to cast extra light on their meaning?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given my comment in respect of all the conversations I heard. The persons whose voices I recognised, the content of what they were saying. I think that I gave my view on each and every one of them. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's take one. I'm trying to avoid going through them all, or at least even a significant number of them, Mr. Babic. But let's take the intercept that is recorded as having been between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik at -- I was looking for a date, Mr. Babic, but it's undated. But you said you thought the date for the particular conversation was the 15th or 16th of May, 1991. So it's actually tab 1 of the intercept -- the intercepts that you were asked to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be given that. I'm not sure physically where this item is. It was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more precise, Mr. Stewart, as to where to find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in the schedule which was attached, as we understand it, attached to his witness statement. It's detached now physically in my papers, but that's another matter. Perhaps Mr. Tieger can -- it looks as if he's about to help. It looks as if he's eager to help at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you assist us, Mr. Tieger? We have had these comments on the telephone tabs in -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that it could perhaps be put on the ELMO and then be enlarged. Madam Usher, could you please put it. It's the top -- the first entry on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, although the individual intercept transcripts have not yet been distributed, I've indicated earlier that they would be available, and at least we have one -- we have a number of such copies. If that is the nature of counsel's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we please zoom in on the top entry and a little bit more to the right, so that the comment -- this is the one, I take it, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour. It's exactly that. I think the date for this conversation is 15th or 16th May. That's exactly it, Your Honour. And the -- yes, in part because the reference to the Presidency session at which Mesic was not elected. Although then my practical question related to the actual -- the transcript itself and its physical whereabouts. I have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was indicating that copies of the actual transcript are available and we can provide them now if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we put -- is there -- is there no copy available at this moment? It's also in the Treanor binder? It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Essentially, we can either move for their admission or we can refer back to the position we were in when they were marked originally, which is that they weren't physically marked but they were considered part of the package and would be physically provided before they were moved into admission. So they are here now physically and we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're here physically. Let's just, for the support of the questions put by Mr. Stewart, try to identify its -- could we then have the -- Madam Usher, could you please return that to us so we know where to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give the B/C/S original to the witness and we'll have the English translation on the ELMO. This is material which has not yet been admitted into evidence. Let's -- we'll just use it at this moment as a document which could be either marked for identification or admitted into evidence at a later stage. I think we need that in evidence, as a matter of fact. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As indicated, and I hope this is clear, all of the intercepts accompany the appropriate declarations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have not given a number -- numbers yet, but it's identified. It's number 1 on the list which appears on page 7 as an annex to the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give the binder already a number. There's no decision yet taken as to the admission, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P154A, the binder of intercept transcripts accompanying the statement P154, with 33 tabs. And P154B, the CD-ROM of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Everything being on the ELMO, Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, your summary of -- or your comments on this particular intercept are, first of all, you think the date for this conversation is 15th or 16th May 1991, in part because of the reference to the Presidency session at which Mesic was not elected. So there you're effectively talking about a checkable historical event which enables us to date the document, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are able to supply the name of the person who was drowned; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you know that that person of that name was drowned, and you suppose it must be him they're talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Vukasin Soskocanin. I knew that he had purportedly drowned, purportedly. But I did hear other information about this as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, those are the rumours that you refer to, aren't they? That's the other information you're talking about. That's what you refer to about the rumours that he was killed by his own men or the state security was involved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dead. Allegedly he had drowned in the Danube. And people who had had contacts with him and others were Borovo Selo told me that it was the DB, the state security, that had killed him. But I did not hear about this as a rumour but as a serious piece of information at the time when I heard about this, and this was at the actual time when it occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Babic. I want to show you another document which comes from a book in this case. We have copies of this, Your Honour. And for the record, I will say, of course, what the book is. It's a book written by Adam LeBor and LeBor is all one word, L-e-b-o-r but the L and the B are capitalised. Adam LeBor who's a -- an apparently English journalist, has worked for the Independent and the Times, among other things. It's called "Milosevic, a biography." And it was published in 2002, first published in Great Britain in 2002. And we've copied, in accordance with what we understand to be the usual practice, we've copied the page before and the page after, as well as the particular page containing the passage which I want to put to Mr. Babic. It's written in English, not surprisingly, Mr. LeBor. The particular passage is in the middle of page 228, and the period being talked about is May 1995 or the summer of 1995. Faced just -- well, Mr. Babic may know enough English to be able to identify the paragraph, but it won't help anyway because we understand that he doesn't sufficiently read English. So it says: "Faced with the" -- please listen, Mr. Babic: "Faced with the capture of sector west the international community proposed a plan known as Z-4, considering the future events of that summer of 1995, Z-4 offered unimaginable benefits to the rebel Serbs, including self-determination, their own flag, police, parliament, and a president." And the Serbs being talked about here are the Krajina Serbs in your Krajina, Mr. Babic. "Milosevic supported the plan, as did Tudjman, although with reservations. In a decision of quite remarkable stupidity, the Krajina Serb leaders Milan Martic and Milan Babic, rejected Z-4 outright. Instead, they dispatched troops to join the Bosnian Serb's army attack on the Bosnian government-held city of Bihac. Bihac, cut off by besieging Serbs, had been declared a UN safe area, like Srebrenica, when Srebrenica fell in July, the Bosnian Serb military leader, General Ratko Mladic, launched an attack on Bihac." And then it's correct, isn't it, Mr. Babic, that that was all a military disaster for the Serbs, wasn't it, as it turned out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you quoted just now is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was tragic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... whether the military outcome was a disaster. No one asked you to confirm that it was a stupid decision or not. It's not -- that's a totally different matter. The only question put to you now is whether the military result was a disaster. Would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Your Honour, but all sorts of things were said here, and all sorts of things were quoted that are incorrect. So I do not find the question itself to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, as such, I repeated it, I think, is quite clear. You can forget about all the rest, whether stupid, whether you took that decision, whatever happened: Was the military result a disaster? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this concern Bihac or something else? I don't understand the question yet again. What does it specifically refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It specifically refers to the attack on Bihac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a disaster. It was a military defeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you agree --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Babic, that your rejection of the plan known as Z-4 was, therefore, also, as it turned out, a serious error?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to tell me whether you are saying "you" in the singular or in the plural. I accepted it. Others did not. The question was whether the rejection of the plan contributed to what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right, Mr. Babic. Let's get it clear, then. When this book refers to a decision of quite remarkable stupidity and then to the Krajina Serb leaders Milan Martic and Milan Babic rejecting Z-4 outright, are you saying that the book is wrong, that you personally did not reject the Z-4 proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It's not that I did not reject it. I accepted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But -- well, what's come across in the translation, these negatives again. You said: "It's not that I did not reject it. I accepted it." So -- yes. It's not that I rejected it. You're saying you accepted it. The book is wrong. That's what you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, it is not only that he did not reject it. He accepted it as a matter of fact. It's a question of emphasis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear, Mr. Babic, you accepted the Z-4 plan. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm certainly not going to enter into a quarrel with the interpreters about that, Your Honour. I'll accept what they say about all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's been three times confirmed now, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Your Honours will give me one moment. That deals with that point, Your Honour, and concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Tieger, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two relatively small matters. Unfortunately, I think one may take a little more time to address than the other. Let me begin with that one, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, directing your attention to the military document dated December 26th, 1991, that was the subject of discussion earlier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I note that there was at least some discussion about this document during the course of one of your earlier transcribed interviews, and this is tape 10 -- 14 in the period -- on January 14th, 2002, on page 56. And in the middle of the page, you indicate that you wanted to explain the order and that identified the order explained that on December 26 you were the president of Republika Srpska Krajina. In that capacity, I'm paraphrasing now, commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska Krajina -- I'd like to move forward on this. You explain something about the document, including the stamp in the upper left corner, which indicates the autonomous region of Srpska Krajina, staff of Territorial Defence. So it means that this document was drafted in the staff headquarters of TO of Srpska Krajina. You then go on to say that you don't remember the exact point of time, but it must be somewhere about this time, that is, when the relevant operational zones were set up. And now I continue quoting: "Now Colonel Radoslav Maksic, who was the commander of the chief central staff of TO, he brought to me a document in which it was either determined or ordered, or it was an order or instruction, I don't know what type, so it was a kind of an order on the movement, shifting certain artillery units which had the range to reach Zagreb. And he said that I ought to sign that and that this be my order, and I remember that I signed a document, this kind, this content. So to my recollection, this document corresponded to that activity. I did think it over about the circumstances under which this happened, this occurred. It was the time of the debate concerning the Vance Plan, namely, the time the debate on deployment of UN peace forces in the area of the Krajina. You see, even after today, I ask myself why did I, who wasn't involved in the operations of -- in the operational aspects of the units and the operational activities, that I signed and gave my approval that such action be taken on the movement of artillery. It could mean provocation in connection with the activities going on surrounding the Vance Plan. As I see it today, that was foolish. I think that also then my feelings weren't [phoen] of this nature, namely that the obstruction would be carried out in this way. Nonetheless, I did sign such document for Maksic. However, didn't dare not to agree in order to avoid creating an enemy against me out of a person who belongs to the Milosevic group of people, not because of the person himself but to the line that was leading to Milosevic. It was a type of direct personal relationship leading out, and it wasn't a matter of general public discussion. I signed this for Maksic not wanting to impose primarily that. This is my recollection and my feelings. Well, my conclusion today is rather different from what it was at that time. Looking upon those events from today's point, probably I wouldn't proceed in this way. This a later wisdom that started, began developing, having a clear sight of it from 1994 onwards and since March 1992 I already had some different views concerning these events." Mr. Babic, does that passage assist you in any way in refreshing your recollection or in otherwise illuminating this document and your role in it for the benefit of the Court?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing is I still believe that the purpose of all this was to compromise me as a negotiator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, my second question is directed to the meeting in Bosanski Novi sometime around the late summer of 1992. Mr. Stewart indicated that in an earlier interview there was reference to a joint assembly session of the assemblies of Republika Srpska and RSK. I note that in your statement, you refer to a meeting at which you arrived late and refer to the event in Bosanski Novi in the late summer of 1992 three times as a meeting. Can you tell us whether or not it is your recollection that that meeting was a joint assembly session, some other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. kind of meeting, or can you illuminate that in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was some sort of meeting. As I mentioned, somebody told me that it was a session of the joint assembly, but that did not look like it. It was some sort of meeting. It did not look to me like a joint session of the assembly, or rather, a session of the joint assembly. It looked to me like a very large meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If I could have one more moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Since nothing new has been introduced in this re-examination -- is there -- no, nothing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're accepting that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to be certain that I've followed your evidence correctly. I seem to have heard you saying today, and I quote, when you were talking about Mr. Branko Kostic, you said, and I quote you in English: [In English] "Technically speaking, he was the leading or he played the leading role or the leading role belonged to him." [Interpretation] In this context, concerning Mr. Krajisnik, you said: [In English] "Had a representative role. I don't remember him playing an active part." [Interpretation] I would appreciate it if you would explain what you mean by these two comments about these two persons. Do you mean to say that Mr. Krajisnik, in a certain area, had no more than a representative role and did not actually play an active part, or what is it that you actually mean, precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I meant exclusively and specifically only that one meeting held in the palace of the Federation on the 23rd of October, 1991. I meant that technically it was chaired by Mr. Branko Kostic. He was the chairman. And I believe I already mentioned in my evidence that Slobodan Milosevic was actually behind all that. And as far as Momcilo Krajisnik is concerned, I did say these two things. He had a representative role, he had the capacity and the authority to represent the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And when I said that he did not play an active part, I meant the meeting itself. I don't remember him taking the floor and discussing or making speeches. That's what I meant. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. My second question could be much simpler. If I understand correctly, you were the president of the SDS party, beginning with 1994 in Krajina, I mean -- 1992, that is. Was that after the death of Mr. Raskovic? Isn't it? And for the rest of the year of 1992, you were president of the SDS party of Krajina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me clarify. Until the 29th of November, 1992, I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, presided by Mr. Jovan Raskovic. That party had its regional board for SAO Krajina and I was a member of that regional board. I was at the same time president of the municipal board of that party for Knin. After the death of Mr. Jovan Raskovic on the 29th of November, 1992, a group of members of the Serbian Democratic Party, presided by Mr. Raskovic, a group from Krajina, that is, established an independent Serbian Democratic Party of Krajina, of which I became president. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But it is the same party as the SDS, which existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or was it another part party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was another party. It was not the same as the SDS. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] That is to say, it was a question only of name; there was no identity, no relationship between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Those were separate parties. But even the names were not identical. The names were different. The party in Bosnia-Herzegovina was called the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina and was later renamed into the Serbian Democratic Party of Serbian Lands. Whereas the party led by Raskovic was the Serbian Democratic Party, and the party that I presided over and which I helped establish, was the Serbian Democratic Party of Krajina. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] All right. Did you then, if I understand well, did your party, the SDS, have any relations with the SDS party which existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you coordinate, for instance, your actions, mutually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There were certain attempts for our SDS party of Krajina to be included in the SDS party in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that did not happen. Our party -- parties were in fact opposed, my party and the Karadzic's SDS party. They were conflicting parties. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] My final question, then: It seemed to me that your relations were rather looking -- you were rather looking towards Belgrade, towards the Republic of Serbia, rather than Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you, and I hope that the interpreters would grant us perhaps five to ten minutes extra so that we could conclude rather than to have to resume next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first ask you a rather general question. Really sensitive issues, were they ever put on paper? And when I say "really sensitive issues," include hidden agendas. Because you spoke about meeting with others where you were invited, not on paper, but invited orally or by telephone, and you would have discussions on sensitive issues. Could you tell us something about to what extent these kind of sensitive issues, that is, also the means to be used to achieve political aims. I'm not specifically talking about your political aims, but more in general. Would that be put on paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that it was put on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see it to be put on paper, matters you considered of a sensitive nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that it was for reasons of secrecy that you would not find those issues on paper? You're nodding, Mr. Babic, but that doesn't appear on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another question for you. You told us about the use of the Ekavian language, and why would someone use the Ikavian [phoen] language to emphasise it as a unifying factor for Serbs if that would also be the language which was used by Croats, or, and that's an alternative question, or is that exactly why you considered this emphasis to be foolish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is rather a long question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I'm inviting you, more or less, to either explain how this emphasis could be used as a unifying factor or to tell me that that's exactly what you find so foolish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for unification, it was a case of imposing on the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia of a certain linguistic standard that prevailed in Serbia, although I did say that as far as communication is concerned, it is the same language. However, that particular linguistic standard was valid in Serbia. In that sense, unification would mean adapting or adjusting to the linguistic standard prevailing in Serbia. And what was the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was -- I think your testimony was also that it was also used, that same language, by Croats. So if I would choose something to emphasise the unification among -- well, specific people, I would choose something that's exclusive for that group and not used by others as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was exclusively used by Serbs. The Ekavian dialect. Muslims and Croats did not use the Ekavian dialect or pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I haven't got the transcript here literally, but either I misunderstood or it has appeared wrongly in the transcript. I do not know, but the matter is clear to me now. May I ask you another -- you told us about documents you gave to the investigators, and you made a distinction between two types of documents, the one you found in the archives and the others -- yes, you seem to have with you and which you did not have to seek in the archives. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both types of document originated from the archives, but they were in my possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but some of them you had already, or -- because it's -- my question would be: Why did you take them with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had one type of document that was from the archive in Knin. That related to the legal status of Krajina, and this category encompassed a large number of documents, and I took them because the counsellor, the advisor of the Yasushi Akashi, the then-civilian representative of the UNPROFOR for Yugoslavia, Yelena Guskova, asked me for that type of document. She was interested as a historian. And I had that in my possession ready to be given to her. That's why I had them and that's why they stayed with me. The other category of documents remained in the bureau of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Belgrade, that bureau, that office, was abolished in 1996. That is another type of document that I possessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That explains why you had the other documents in your possession which did not directly come from the archives in Belgrade. Thank you, Mr. Babic. You said at a certain moment during your testimony that there was more to add on the subject of the impression on what Karadzic actually had in mind at the Celinac meeting. Could you tell us what there was more to add to what you have already told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can clarify, maybe, what it meant. It meant that he would create a unified Serbian territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina by expelling Muslims. That's what it referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was your impression. I mean, so what you add is that the means by which you would create that situation is by compelling Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a bit more insight on what this impression was based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is based on the fact that at that time there were communities of municipalities, like Serbian areas, created by the leadership of the Serbian democratic parties. These areas were separated. There was no way that, according to the principle of majority and referendi they could be united. That's why that attempt failed and that's why Karadzic was against this voting based on the majority principle that was used in Krajina. Because that majority principle would foil his aspiration to unite these territories where Serbs were a minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these answers. Have the questions of the Bench raised any need for further questions to Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's not for the Defence either, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I was looking at both parties, as a matter of fact. Then, Mr. Babic, this concludes your evidence at this moment. Usually I say to witnesses goodbye and I hope -- in this case, I cannot fully exclude that you would be recalled, although it's not what I expect at this moment, but I cannot exclude that. So, therefore, whether I say thank you for coming and whether I should say thank you for coming and -- well, it's not a kind of language, we'll meet again, don't know where, don't know when. So this is just to avoid any wrong impression that this was the last time you would appear here in this -- before this Chamber, who is assigned to deal with the case against Mr. Krajisnik. Nevertheless, thank you for answering questions of both parties and of the Bench, and you may be now escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to that document from the book, I think I forgot to ask Ms. Philpott is reminding us that it needs a number and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we need the presence of the witness for your next comments, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd ask Mr. Babic to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mueller, you're also excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For what still has to be said by the parties, do we have to remain in closed session, apart from whether we should have ever gone in closed session, Mr. Stewart? If not, then we'll return into -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, difficult for me to know whether the Court wishes this in private -- in closed session or not, but since it's part of the entire proceeding, it seems to make more sense to me. I just want to move into admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, we are stealing time already from another Trial Chamber. I suggest to the parties that we deal with all the technicalities just at the beginning of the next session, which would be, I think, next Monday, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we deal with all these technical materials, if there are any numbers, et cetera, next Monday, so then we can properly prepare for it and we don't have to do it in a rush. Is there anything else to be said at this moment? No. Then we briefly return into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We're in open session again. I -- in this open session, I repeat what has been said in closed session before today, that an oral decision has been given by the Chamber this morning on a confidential motion which was not opposed by the Defence, in which videolink and closed session was granted. That was the fourth motion. I take it that just the content of the motion was confidential and not the existence of the motion, Mr. Tieger. Is that a proper understanding? Because otherwise I would have to ask the transcript to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that's the correct understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So nothing has to be corrected. Then if the parties would get in touch with the -- not with the Senior Legal Officer but with Mr. De Hemptinne, to see whether we could, since we have a break of a couple of days now and the Chamber has received suggestions by the parties on how to proceed, especially on from the 24th of June, and if you could find an opportunity to just briefly exchange views and see whether the -- what the Chamber has in mind, and this is just a matter of scheduling and to see whether we should spend more time on hearing evidence in court or whether we should leave more time to the parties to communicate in order to avoid unnecessary presentation of evidence in court. If you'd make yourself available this afternoon, that would be highly appreciated. I announced that for last Friday, but finally I thought it better to delay it until today. Is there anything else the parties would want to raise in this already stolen time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Still 15 seconds. Your Honour knows that the -- what Your Honour has just described as the ambit of any proposed meeting this afternoon is not the extent of the ambit which the Defence suggests should be considered. Your Honour, I'll say it more clearly, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Your Honour hasn't mentioned time for preparation of the defence case, which you know has been a continuing issue, and that is very much at the forefront of what the Defence has in mind in all such discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's say that if views are exchanged on how to use time, one could also exchange views on what to use that time for, and of course the position of the Defence is not unknown to the Chamber. Then we'll adjourn with a special thanks to the technicians and the interpreters, which helped us out, and already apologies for the other Trial Chamber for stealing 13 minutes of their time. We'll adjourn until Monday, the 14th of June, 9.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
